title: How do you generate sounds/music for your games?
author: uchilles2020
selftext: Wondering if anyone has suggestions on how to generate good sound effects and music for AI games? Opus 5 does great work with graphics but can't seem to get great results on sounds.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body:
Yes, plenty of musicians can make tracks for you for free or almost free, and they’ll still be better than anything AI generates - boring / generic.  
And there’s nothing wrong with using free music either. You’re not an AAA studio and you’re not Kojima. You’ll most likely make a mediocre game that even great music wouldn’t be able to save.

replies.author: vurt72
replies.body:
"and they’ll still be better than anything AI generates"  
I have my doubts. If an artist creates free music for you or for a few dollars it will not be close to as good... I think the same for art actually, AI can do amazing art as well, but you do have to try to keep it consistent etc or people will directly notice. AI music can also sound garbage if you do not know what you are doing, but for both of these - if you are that clueless then game dev will likely not be your thing in the end.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body:
In practice, everything AI generates has consistency problems. An LLM isn't actually intelligent at all - even a lizard has more intelligence than an LLM. There is no intent or meaning behind what AI generates. An LLM is literally just predicting what comes next, with no understanding of the meaning of either the words or the sentences made from them.

I can understand using AI for 2D/3D content because the alternative can be prohibitively expensive. But music is a completely different case. A game doesn't need hundreds or thousands of tracks - often 10-20 is enough. It's easy to find suitable existing music, and it's often free or almost free. So there is simply no reason to replace one element of your game with content that is bad.

replies.author: vurt72
replies.body:
Token Prediction is a small part of how the model actually works. They are far beyond human comprehension at this point, we understand very little of how they work, not even the best scientist in the field of AI understands how they work fully.   
But we are understanding some parts. This is a cool overview, i suggest you to watch:  
[The different levels of how Claude thinks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rKV5JcALQoQ)  
its only 5 mins

For my recent game i made a synthesizer engine, then an engine to do generative music, the music in the game is never the same, always different.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body: That is a major part of how it works. Don't give me marketing bullshit. Anyone who has actually interacted with LLMs has seen them do exceptionally stupid things. LLMs do not possess intelligence, and anyone looking for intelligence in them is either selling AI services or is a fool.

replies.author: vurt72
replies.body:
Not marketing, they were open with faults as well.   
It's like saying "Chess is just choose the next move" but not taking into account the actual thinking. It leaves out a lot.   
  
But yes its a large part but there is architecture, training data, post-training, reasoning methods, context handling, tools, retrieval, decoding... the most interesting part is that this combined leads to emergent behavior of the AI, all in all gets so complex that humans can not understand it.   
So yes the are immensely intelligent.

For the last 3 years i have used them daily. Almost every week there is something that amazes me. One recent thing that happened, i had a image file called lower.png, the AI worked with something else in that folder. i was about to write a long prompt of what i wanted it to do with this lower.png file, quite an advanced implementation for how the graphics should work using this image.   
  
After it was done with the current work it was doing it said "I also found lower.png in the folder and i implemented it" without me even saying what it was for, how i wanted the graphics to work etc. Quite amazing, it just looked at the image and drew its own conclusions. Seen it quite a few times, but that is a recent one.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body:
At their core, LLMs are prediction systems. You can deny reality, but that won't change it. Again, this mechanism plays a key role in how an LLM works and in the kind of output it produces. Of course there are nuances, but this is one of its fundamental, system-defining properties.

You should stop listening to Big Tech marketing. Big Tech companies literally brag like children about how their LLM supposedly "escaped" somewhere and hacked something. Meanwhile, some of those same "genius" LLMs are deleting production databases, while technical debt has grown to previously unimaginable levels.

There is no intelligence there. It is literally a mathematical function. Stop talking nonsense. You might as well start talking to a power drill and convince yourself that it has a mind.

replies.author: vurt72
replies.body:
one could argue humans are prediction systems too, an advanced race beyond humans might think its all we are, not caring about underlaying nuances or not thinking they play in a lot for the outcome of how we think or act. 

its hardly bragging, it caused huge security concerns and there is a lot of talking now of wanting them to stop developing it further. how would it bragging lol? its like saying Tesla brags when their car crashes due to malfunction. How would that work, it doesn't. It doesnt impress apart from the fact that the tech is advanced and therefore hard to predict. The dangers are real, why would a company want something that can go rogue? They will stay the hell away. 

The intelligence is undeniable and from here it will just get better, from the 3 years i have used its a been a mind blowing ride, and this tech might not have evolved beyond 1% its very hard to tell...  They only thing i know is that current models will be laughable in a year, like how last years models today seem "cute" at most.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body:
You can argue whatever you want, but humans are not prediction systems, and drawing parallels between humans and LLMs is silly.

It is bragging, and that should be obvious to anyone over the age of 20.

The claim that there is intelligence there isn't just questionable. Yann LeCun, literally one of the leading scientists in the field, has said that scaling and further progress of LLMs will not lead to recreating intelligence.

LLMs are definitely useful, but they are nowhere near as intelligent as you've convinced yourself they are. All you've actually done is create a pile of technical debt; you just don't have enough expertise to realize it.

replies.author: vurt72
replies.body:
He thinks its not the right tech to advance to AGI, and its possible of course. Again, we might have advanced 1% into AI, impossible to day.

What exists today as LLM's is extremely intelligent in comparison to just 1 year ago, i follow this super closely + again i use this daily for many hours, my expertise comes from that, its impossible to not see just how intelligent it is.

comments.author: Evoroth
comments.body:
I already did chip tunes for a game and then created a Python script to turn those into better quality tracks. 

I’ve then turned that into a skill for AI for things in the future and it’s worked great for placeholder tracks - ultimately all building tracks and effects with Python and the output being ogg. 

There’s lots of less involved options too though like others have mentioned: pixabay, suno, etc. there’s also the free GDV libraries from Soniss

comments.author: sevenoutdb
comments.body: For VO, I'm using the first paid tier (US$7?) for elevenlabs. I think I'll get something like 80 lines of finished dialogue for the 40k tokens I get a month, because I will get some wonkly mispronunciations and I'll spend a few thousand credites creating custom character voices. For music/SFX - I've purchased several audio packs with indie-game friendly distribution licenses over the years with both SFX and music, so I'm picking the best of what I got for what I need for my game these and spelunking through old email receipts to confirm the usage rights before I ship the game.

comments.author: WantedRogue

I use Elevenlabs for sound effects and Suno for music. Just make sure you have the necessary license. Any effects or music you generate before you have the correct license can’t be used even if you subsequently buy the license. 

I find Elevenlabs to be a bit fiddly, I end up use Gemini to help me get the right prompt. Without a paid tier I burn through tokens. There may be a better sound effects AI.

comments.author: uchilles2020
comments.body:
Thanks for the suggestions everyone!

Here's what I am trialing, based on your suggestions.

1. Connect to elevenlabs for audio
2. Ask to create asset library with sounds so I can check individually
3. Get short videos for a reference game with sound I like - one with music only, one with gameplay sounds + music, one with music off and sfx only - max 2 mins each 
4. Ask to connect to Gemini to check sounds (Claude can't do this) and give detailed feedback on sound and vibe
5. Then ask Claude to check against reference to loop and improve till quality bar is met.

In short, trying to see if I can build a gauntlet loop for audio. Will share outcome next week.

comments.author: alexid95
comments.body: one thing I'd add: match loudness on every candidate before Gemini judges it. Otherwise the loop can keep rewarding “better” audio that's mostly just louder, while missing seams or clipping.

What kind of game are you building?
